title: Quantum games PCP with efficient honest provers and short messages
formal: Does every promise problem \(\mathrm{L}=(\mathrm{L}_{\mathrm{yes}},\mathrm{L}_{no})\) in QMA admit a one-round entangled multiprover proof with a uniform classical polynomial-time verifier, a constant number r of provers and polylogarithmic-length classical questions and answers, such that: \((i)\) on every \(x\in \mathrm{L}_{\mathrm{yes}}\), some polynomial-size quantum witness permits uniform quantum polynomial-time preparation and local execution of an honest strategy accepted with probability at least \(2/3\); and \((ii)\) on every \(x\in \mathrm{L}_{no}\), every entangled strategy, with no computational bound on the dishonest provers, is accepted with probability at most \(1/3\)?
why: Would connect efficient verification of quantum witnesses to succinct classical interaction with entangled provers. The honest-prover requirement preserves the computational meaning of the witness, which unrestricted entangled proof-system containments do not ensure.
status_note: The full CCC 2026 question and the 2024 status note were checked, with subsequent searches through 11 September 2026. No matching efficient-prover protocol or impossibility theorem was located. The stronger logarithmic-question/constant-answer conjecture is distinguished explicitly.

progress.text: The status note formalizes witness-assisted efficient provers and explains why the earlier claimed quantum games PCP construction does not establish the conjecture.
The CCC paper proves streaming gap amplification and explicitly leaves efficient-prover games with polylogarithmic questions and answers open.

sentences: The question asks whether every quantum-verifiable problem has a short classical game with entangled provers.
Both questions and answers must have polylogarithmic length, with a constant completeness–soundness gap.
Honest provers must prepare their entanglement and answer in polynomial time given copies of a polynomial-size witness.
Soundness must hold even against computationally unrestricted cheating provers.
Existing unrestricted entangled proof systems and the source’s streaming Hamiltonian result do not establish this efficient-prover communication target.

definitions: Write \(n=|x|\). QMA consists of promise problems whose YES instances have polynomial-qubit quantum witnesses accepted by a uniform polynomial-time quantum verifier with probability at least \(2/3\), while every witness on a NO instance is accepted with probability at most \(1/3\). In the requested game, a classical verifier samples correlated questions, sends one to each of r noncommunicating provers, receives one classical answer from each, and decides acceptance in polynomial time. The provers may share entanglement prepared before the questions arrive. For each L, r and an exponent a are fixed independently of n, and every individual message has at most \(O((\log (n+2))^{a})\) bits. Honest efficiency includes a uniform quantum polynomial-time setup algorithm which, given x and polynomially many copies of a polynomial-qubit state \(\psi _{x}\), prepares the shared state, followed by uniform quantum polynomial-time local response algorithms. The state \(\psi _{x}\) is an existential witness depending on x, not a supplied circuit for preparing it. Soundness quantifies over arbitrary local quantum strategies with arbitrary finite-dimensional shared entanglement; only communication after separation is forbidden. There is no promise on inputs outside \(\mathrm{L}_{\mathrm{yes}}\cup \mathrm{L}_{no}\). The fixed gap can be amplified by a constant number of repetitions without changing the polylogarithmic communication scale. The question imposes no logarithmic bound on the verifier’s total random bits and no additional cryptographic assumption.
answer_criterion: Construct the stated protocol for every QMA promise problem, proving both witness-assisted honest efficiency and soundness against unrestricted entangled provers; or prove that at least one QMA promise problem has no such protocol. A protocol with polynomial-length answers, or one whose honest entanglement cannot be prepared efficiently from a polynomial witness, does not meet this target.

context_blocks.title: A verifier asks much less than the full proof
context_blocks.text: The verifier has an n-bit instance but exchanges only polylogarithmically many bits with each prover. Quantum information stays with the provers. The task is to check a quantum witness through these short classical exchanges, with a constant separation between acceptance on YES and NO instances.

context_blocks.title: Efficiency includes preparing the shared state
context_blocks.text: It is insufficient for a prover to answer quickly after receiving an arbitrarily difficult-to-prepare entangled state. The setup itself must take polynomial time given copies of a polynomial-size witness. Conversely, cheating provers receive no time or entanglement-size restriction.

context_blocks.title: Ordinary MIP* containment does not supply the missing condition
context_blocks.text: Very powerful entangled proof systems already exist when honest provers are unrestricted. The 2024 status note explains why these results do not establish efficient-prover quantum games PCP and identifies an error in an earlier claimed QMA construction.

context_blocks.title: The source asks for a weaker communication target than the strongest conjecture
context_blocks.text: The status note proposes \(O(\log  n)\)-bit questions and \(O(1)\)-bit answers. The selected CCC passage explicitly asks for polylogarithmic questions and answers. Resolving this card would settle that weaker efficient-prover benchmark, without automatically establishing the stronger message lengths.

context_blocks.title: Streaming verification leaves an answer-length gap
context_blocks.text: The 2026 paper proves a streaming Hamiltonian verification result. It discusses a possible game application with short questions but polynomial-size answers; that application is not a theorem in the checked passage, and even those parameters would not meet this card’s answer bound.
